plan.contextChunk:
$$c_{u,v}\left[n,m\right] = A \cos \left(2 \pi \left( \frac{u\,n}{N}  + \frac{v\,m}{M}  \right) \right)$$
where $A$ is the amplitude and $u$ and $v$ are the two spatial
frequencies and define how fast or slow the waves change along the
spatial dimensions $n$ and $m$. @fig-disc2Dsignal shows some examples.


![2D sine waves with $N=M=20$. The frequency values are (a) $u=2, v=0$; (b) $u=3, v=1$; (c) $u=7,v=-5$.](figures/Image_processing_fourier/disc2Dsignal.png){#fig-disc2Dsignal}

### Complex Exponentials

Another important signal is the complex exponential wave:
$$e_{u}\left[n\right] = \exp \left(2 \pi j   \frac{u\, n}{N}   \right)$$

Complex exponentials are related to cosine and sine waves by Euler's
formula: $$
\exp \left(j a\right) = \cos (a) + j \sin (a)$${#eq-euler} @fig-complexexponential
shows the one dimensional (1D) discrete complex exponential function
(for $v=0$). As the values are complex, the plot shows in the $x$-axis
the real component and in the $y$-axis the imaginary component. As $n$
goes from 0 to $N-1$ the function rotates along the complex circle of
unit magnitude.


![Complex exponential wave with (a) $N=40$, $k=1$, $A=1$; and (b) $N=40$, $k=3$, $A=1$. The red and green curves show the real and imaginary waves. The black line is the complex exponential. The dots correspond to the discrete samples.](figures/Image_processing_fourier/complexexponential.png){width="80%" #fig-complexexponential}

In 2D, the complex exponential wave is
$$e_{u,v}\left[n,m\right] = \exp \left(2 \pi j \left(  \frac{u\, n}{N}  + \frac{v\,m}{M}  \right) \right)$$where $u$ and $v$ are the two spatial frequencies. Note that complex
exponentials in 2D are separable. This means they can be written as the
product of two 1D signals:
$$e_{u,v}\left[n,m\right]   = e_{u}\left[n\right] e_{v}\left[m\right]$$

A remarkable property is that the complex exponentials form an
orthogonal basis for discrete signals and images of finite length. For
images of size $N \times M$,
$$\left<e_{u,v}, e_{u',v'} \right> = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} e_{u,v}\left[n,m\right] e^*_{u',v'}\left[n,m\right] = MN \delta \left[u-u'\right]\delta \left[v-v'\right]$$
Therefore, any finite length discrete image can be decomposed as a
linear combination of complex exponentials.

## The Discrete Fourier Transform

demo_steps.narration: With frequency u=1, the complex exponential wave completes exactly one full 360-degree rotation along the 40-sample path. The red real projection shows a single cosine cycle, and the green imaginary projection shows a single sine cycle.

demo_steps.title: Winding Faster (u = 3)
demo_steps.narration: As u increases to 3, the helix winds three times faster, completing exactly three full turns. The real (red) and imaginary (green) waves now oscillate with three times the spatial frequency, demonstrating how 'u' controls the wave's speed of change.

demo_steps.title: Maximum Frequency (u = 5)
demo_steps.narration: At u=5, the 3D spiral completes five rotations. All projections, continuous curves, and discrete samples recalculate dynamically to show the perfect synchronization of the 3D helical wave with its orthogonal 2D projections.

plan.view_reasoning: (1) The dominant baseline is the n-axis (propagation axis), which in the source diagram runs diagonally from the upper-left toward the lower-right, receding into the screen. (2) This receding baseline implies a camera placed at an angle relative to the axis (around 45-65 degrees azimuth) to preserve the helical appearance rather than collapsing it. (3) The vertical Imaginary axis points straight up and the Real axis is horizontal, indicating a modest elevation angle of around 20 degrees is used to separate the horizontal and vertical projection planes clearly without making either too shallow.

evaluation.interactivity_usability_analysis: The developer implemented several high-quality, functional, and pedagogically useful interactions: (1) A frequency slider (u) that dynamically recalculates and updates the 3D helix path, 2D sine/cosine projections, sample spheres, and projection lines. (2) Comprehensive raycasting interactions via `registerInteractive` on all key geometries (curves, connector lines, axes, and individual sample dots) showing tailored educational popups (e.g., displaying the exact computed complex coordinates for clicked sample dots). (3) A guided step-through system (`goToStep`) that transitions camera angles (e.g., orthographic side-view to a collapsed unit-circle face-on view) and updates narration text. (4) A double-click canvas listener to transition between demo steps.
evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis:
Core concept: 1D discrete complex exponential wave $e_u[n] = \exp(2\pi j u n / N)$ and its decomposition via Euler's formula into real (cosine) and imaginary (sine) components. 
User-visible claims evaluated:
1. Slider 'u' adjusts the spatial frequency: accurate, matches the textbook's description of how frequency scales oscillations.
2. "The red cosine and green sine projections..." (narration/tooltips): accurate, correctly identifies the real and imaginary components under Euler's formula.
3. Axis labels ('I', 'R', 'n') and numeric scales: accurate, correctly mapping the propagation index $n$ and the complex components in 3D space.
4. "every sample satisfies R² + I² = 1" (unit-circle view narration): mathematically correct for a constant-amplitude complex exponential wave.
All geometry, equations, tooltips, and interactive components are conceptually perfectly aligned.
evaluation.notes: The implementation is of exceptional quality, achieving perfect scores in both interactivity and conceptual accuracy. The interactive frequency slider, 3D complex helix, 2D projection lines, raycast-enabled sample dots with educational popups, and the guided step-through system are all perfectly executed and mathematically flawless.
